subtype: Approach: listing everyone's ideas and voting [Thinking]
passage: Mrs Kapoor gave the Class 5 group ten minutes to choose a project topic. Pranav tore a sheet into strips. "Everyone write your idea on a strip." Simran wrote 'water cycle', Omkar wrote 'volcanoes', Tia wrote 'our local birds', and Pranav wrote 'robots'. They laid the strips on the desk and each got two votes. Pranav counted. Water cycle had three, birds had three, robots and volcanoes one each. They voted again between the two, and the water cycle won. Omkar looked at his strip for a moment. Then he shrugged and said, "Okay, I can draw the clouds."

qa.q: How many votes did each child get?
What might Omkar feel when volcanoes lose, and what shows it?
qa.a: Omkar feels a little disappointed; looking at the strip for a moment before shrugging shows it.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the group use, and why?
qa.a: They could combine two ideas into one plan, such as the water cycle with a small volcano model. That way more members would keep a part they care about.

qa.q: How does the vote look to Simran?
qa.a: Simran's water cycle idea won, so the vote probably feels fair and satisfying, and everyone in the group had a say.

grounding: The group writes each child's idea on a paper strip and votes, so everyone gets a say even if the losing idea's owner feels a bit disappointed.

subtype: Approach: listing everyone's ideas and voting [Thinking]
passage:
"We've argued for twenty minutes," said Jaya. "Let's do it properly. Everyone writes their idea on a strip."
Zeenat tore a page into four. "Model volcano." "Chart of rocks." "A short play about an earthquake." "Quiz game."
"Now each of us gets two votes. Tick any two strips, but not your own twice."
Pencils scratched.
"Volcano: four. Play: three. Quiz: one. Chart: zero."
"The chart was mine," said Zeenat quietly.
Jaya looked at her. "Can the volcano have a chart next to it, explaining the layers? You're the best at labels."
Zeenat thought, then half-smiled. "Okay. But I'm doing the lava colours too."

qa.q: How many votes did the volcano get?
How did Zeenat feel when her chart got no votes?
qa.a: Zeenat felt disappointed, saying quietly that the chart was hers.

qa.q: What did Jaya do well after the vote, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She found a place for Zeenat's skill in the winning idea, labels beside the volcano, so the vote didn't leave Zeenat out.

qa.q: How might the rest of the group see the voting?
qa.a: Everyone got two votes and a say, so the result felt fair even to those whose ideas lost.

grounding: Shows a group writing each child's idea on a strip and voting twice each, giving everyone a say though one idea's owner feels disappointed.

subtype: Approach: listing everyone's ideas and voting [Thinking]
passage: Our group of five had argued for three days about the science fair. Everyone thought their own idea was best, and I was tired of it. Then I remembered how my class elects the monitor. At lunch I said, 'Let's each write our idea on a paper strip, and everyone gets two votes.' We had five strips: water filter, solar oven, plant growth, rain gauge, magnet car. I wanted the magnet car. Alka's water filter got five votes; my car got two. I felt a pinch, honestly. But nobody could say it wasn't fair, because everyone had voted. And by Friday we'd built the filter, instead of still arguing. Alka said, 'Nitin, you can do the testing.'

qa.q: How did Nitin feel when the magnet car got two votes?
qa.a: Nitin felt a pinch of disappointment, but accepted it because the vote was fair.

qa.q: Why did voting work better than three days of arguing?
qa.a: Everyone had a say, so nobody could call the result unfair, and the group could finally start building.

qa.q: How might Alka see the vote?
qa.a: Alka's water filter won with five votes, so Alka likely felt pleased and valued, and gave Nitin the testing to do.

grounding: Illustrates a group writing every idea on paper strips and giving each member two votes, which feels fair even to the child whose idea loses.
